lines: Thunder shook the smoker so hard the smoker coughed smoke sideways, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked the smoker, hooks, and food barrels after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the smoker, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the food barrels twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have food barrels to set right.
The first strike sent every animal against the far side of its pen.
Rain came through the smoker vent and turned the ash to paste.
I moved the salt sacks before the roof found another place to leak.
The thunder hid the warning bell, so we passed word door to door.
One flash showed the whole work yard white as bone.
I kept the cleavers off the wall in case another shake knocked them loose.
We ate cold food because nobody trusted a cooking fire during the lightning.
A split branch landed across the pen gate and frightened everything inside.
The hooks rattled for an hour after the worst thunder passed.
I counted livestock at first light, then checked the neighbors.
Water reached the bottom shelf but missed the cured meat.
The children sheltered by the smokehouse because its walls felt solid.
My ears rang so badly I could not hear the rain ease.
We used clean butcher cloths to stop water coming under the door.
The storm left half the firewood wet and every appetite awake.
I checked grease, wood, and hanging meat for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and <dark_gray><wavy>fear</wavy></dark_gray>.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the smoker after.
The smoker can wait. People come first.
We saved what we could reach around the smoker, then stopped pretending things matter more than neighbors.
The smoke is thinning near the smoker, but everyone is still sniffing the air like it might lie.
Grease catches quickly, so I cleared the work yard before carrying water.
We rolled the salt barrels away from the heat before their hoops split.
The livestock smelled smoke early and would not leave the back fence.
I used every clean cloth in the shop on burns and coughing faces.
A spark landed on the smoker roof and nearly gave us a second fire.
Nobody argued when I dumped a whole water barrel across the chopping room.
We fed people from cold stores while the cookfires stayed dark.
The hooks were too hot to touch long after the flames moved on.
I lost a side of meat and gained three neighbors with buckets. Fair trade.
Ash settled on every uncovered surface, even behind the closed doors.
The smokehouse survived because someone kept wetting the outer wall.
I counted people first, animals second, and ruined provisions last.
One ember hid under the fuel pile until nearly dawn.
The village smelled burned for days, but supper returned the next evening.
I have replaced the greasy rags with a lidded bucket since that night.
During a raid, the smoker can go cold. Who makes it behind a door matters more.
The horns stopped, but my hands near the smoker still expect another wave from the road.
We counted living neighbors before the smoker, hooks, and food barrels. That's the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the smoker and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the smoker, I saw fear cross the square. Then I saw courage get there first.
I pulled the livestock into the inner yard before the raiders reached the pens.
We carried smoked food to the cellar so everyone sheltering there could eat.
My cleaver is a work tool, but it held the smokehouse door when the latch broke.
An arrow split the sign above my head while I was dragging a barrel inside.
The raiders tried the back gate and found every butcher in the village waiting.
I passed water and bandages while others held the square.
A frightened cow made more noise than the warning bell.
We rationed the cured meat because nobody knew how long the doors would stay barred.
The smoker went cold during the fighting. Nobody complained.
I knew the raid was ending when I could hear animals over the shouting again.
We found a crossbow bolt buried in the chopping block the next morning.
Every surviving neighbor got a hot meal before I counted what was missing.
The hooks were still swinging when the last horn went quiet.
I have kept extra food below ground since that attack.
Raiders can steal emeralds. They do not get to take our supper too.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the smoker first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the back door by the smoker and listened for anyone calling from the dark.
Dawn gave the smoker enough light to count wounds, missing blocks, and who made it home.
The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping salted meat for the watch between us and teeth.
We are safe enough near the smoker, though every <dark_purple><italic><wavy>shadow</wavy></italic></dark_purple> is being inspected twice.
I woke to the pens going wild before anyone shouted.
The smoker embers gave just enough light to see movement by the back wall.
We brought the children through the work yard because its gate still held.
I kept one hand on the cleaver and the other on the food cellar latch.
Something struck the hanging hooks in the dark and set them clattering.
The livestock would not settle until sunrise showed an empty lane.
We ate slices of cold roast while taking turns at the door.
A broken fence post told me how close the attackers had come.
I knew every neighbor by voice before I could see a single face.
The smell of smoke helped us find the shop when the torches went out.
We blocked the side entrance with the heavy cutting table.
Nobody fetched water alone, even with the well only steps away.
Dawn found muddy tracks circling the animal pens.
I sharpened every blade the next afternoon and hated the sound of it.
For a week, the smallest noise by the smoker woke me.
The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning dust out of the meat barrels.
I checked the smoker, hooks, and food barrels, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the smoker, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
A hard wind teaches a butcher which doors actually close and which ones only pretend.
We are safe enough near the smoker, though the whole village sounds like it is chewing gravel.
Grit worked under every barrel lid no matter how tightly I tied the cloth.
I moved the meat into the cellar before the air turned brown.
The animals pressed against the shelter wall and refused their feed.
Sand stopped the smoker vent until the whole room coughed back at me.
We shared drinking water before using a drop to wash the work tables.
I found one cleaver buried edge down in the yard after the wind eased.
Every strip of uncovered jerky had to be thrown away.
The hooks sounded like bells while the gusts shook the roof.
We tied the pen gates shut with rope when the latches filled with sand.
Nobody wanted supper until we could rinse the grit from our mouths.
I covered my face with an apron and still tasted dust all night.
The smokehouse door vanished behind a drift up to its handle.
We followed the fence from house to house because the lane had disappeared.
Cleaning the salt barrels took longer than cleaning the floor.
The storm passed in hours. I was finding sand in the smoker for weeks.
The smoker can go cold. Warm hands, clear paths, and full hearths come first.
Snow piled against the doors, but everyone near the smoker found shelter.
Cold works quietly around the smoker. We are checking on anyone who stayed quiet too long.
I am clearing snow off the smoker roof and watching for footprints that stop too soon.
We are alright for now near the smoker. Keep the fires fed and the paths open.
I packed extra feed into the pens before the paths disappeared.
The smoker kept one room warm when two hearths ran out of wood.
We hung bright cloth from the doors so nobody walked past shelter in the whiteout.
Snow pressed the animal fence inward until we braced it with the cutting table.
Every hot meal went first to someone who had been clearing paths.
I stored meat outside for once, though I marked it before the drift swallowed it.
The salt stayed dry, which mattered more than anything after the firewood ran low.
We tied a rope from the smokehouse to the well before fetching water.
A calf vanished behind a drift only a few steps from its pen.
The hooks frosted white whenever the door opened.
I checked quiet houses with broth and a shovel.
Nobody traveled alone, even between the shop and the nearest hearth.
The cold made the cleaver handle sting through my gloves.
At dawn, chimney smoke was the only way to count the homes.
When the road reopened, the whole village ate from the same pot.
